title: Unions and Narrowing
summary: Union and literal types, typeof and in checks, and discriminated unions.

steps.title: Union and literal types
body: A **union** `A | B` means "either an A or a B". Combined with **literal types** it replaces most C# enums:
s = "finished";        // error: '"finished"' is not assignable to type 'Status'
`string | null` is how TypeScript models nullability. With `strict` mode on (always turn it on), you cannot use a `string | null` as a `string` until you have checked it.
> **Tip:** TypeScript has an `enum` keyword, but it generates runtime code and Node's type stripping cannot run it. Modern code prefers unions of string literals.

steps.title: Narrowing
body: Inside a check, TypeScript **narrows** the type. The checks it understands:
function len(x: string | string[] | null): number {
return x.length;                       // here x must be string[]
if ("meow" in pet) return pet.meow();  // `in` checks a property exists
Also: `Array.isArray(x)`, `x instanceof Date` (for classes), truthiness (`if (x)`), and early `return`s, which narrow everything after them.

steps.explain: Each check narrows `x` for the code after it, so `x.length` and `x * 2` are safe where they appear.

steps.title: Discriminated unions
body: Give every member of a union a shared **literal** property (the *discriminant*, often `kind` or `type`). Checking it narrows to exactly one member:
case "circle": return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;   // s is the circle here
case "rect":   return s.w * s.h;                 // s is the rect here

This is the single most useful TypeScript pattern. It models API results (`{ ok: true; data } | { ok: false; error }`), loading states, and Redux/React reducer **actions**, which you will build in the project.

steps.title: Format a payment
prompt: Write `describe(p: Payment)` for this discriminated union:
Return `"card ****1234: $5.00"`, `"paypal ada@x.io: $5.00"`, or `"cash: $5.00"` (amount is in cents). Use a `switch` on `method`.

steps.title: Parse API results
prompt: `fetchUser` returns JSON that is either `{ "user": { "name": "Ada" } }` or `{ "error": "message" }`. Write `parseUser(body: unknown): Result` returning a discriminated union:
type Result = { ok: true; name: string } | { ok: false; error: string };
- if `body` is an object with a `user` object that has a string `name`, return `{ ok: true, name }`
- else if it has a string `error`, return `{ ok: false, error }`
- otherwise return `{ ok: false, error: "bad response" }`
starter: type Result = { ok: true; name: string } | { ok: false; error: string };
solution: type Result = { ok: true; name: string } | { ok: false; error: string };
if ("user" in body && typeof body.user === "object" && body.user !== null && "name" in body.user && typeof body.user.name === "string") {
template: Dojo.eq("error", { ok: false, error: "not found" }, parseUser({ error: "not found" }));
Dojo.eq("null", { ok: false, error: "bad response" }, parseUser(null));
Dojo.eq("name not a string", { ok: false, error: "bad response" }, parseUser({ user: { name: 7 } }));
Dojo.eq("a string", { ok: false, error: "bad response" }, parseUser("oops"));
hints: Start with `typeof body === "object" && body !== null` (`typeof null` is "object").
`"user" in body` then lets you read `body.user`, which is still `unknown` until you check it too.
